Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$,
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]). Let
$M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $M \ge 0$ satisfy

$$\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } t \in (a,b).$$

Then

$$\lVert f(b) - f(a)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,(b-a).$$

**No integrability of $f'$ is assumed**, so the theorem applies to every
differentiable $f$; that is why it is proved from the scalar mean value theorem
rather than from
[[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]].
[[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]] records the comparison between the
two routes.

**The equality form is not asserted, and for $m \ge 2$ it is false.** There need
be **no** $\xi \in (a,b)$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$; the companion page
carries a differentiable witness on $[0,1]$. The $\xi$ produced in the proof
below depends on the fixed vector $u = f(b)-f(a)$ and is a mean value point of
the **real** function $t \mapsto \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, not of $f$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Fix $a<b$, an integer $d\ge1$, an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ containing $[a,b]\times$ the states under consideration, and a vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$. $$y'(t)=f(t,y(t))\quad(a\le t\le b),\qquad B(y(a),y(b))=0,$$

where $y$ is a continuously differentiable curve whose graph lies in $\Omega$, whose endpoint pair lies in $D_B$, and where the $d$ scalar components of $B$ give exactly $d$ boundary equations. If the IVP from initial state $s\in\mathbb R^d$ has a unique solution $\phi(\cdot;s)$ on $[a,b]$, the **exact shooting residual** is $R(s):=B(s,\phi(b;s))$ whenever $(s,\phi(b;s))\in D_B$. For a mesh $a=t_0<\cdots<t_N=b$ and segment initial states $s_0,\ldots,s_N$, the **exact multiple-shooting residual** has rows $\phi_i(t_{i+1};s_i)-s_{i+1}$ for $0\le i<N$ and final row $B(s_0,s_N)$, where $\phi_i$ denotes the unique segment IVP solution when it exists. These residuals are defined only on their admissible IVP and boundary domains.

derivations.claim: If the residual vanishes, each row gives $\phi_i(t_{i+1};s_i)=s_{i+1}$. Define $y$ on each interval by the corresponding segment solution. At every interior mesh point, the left endpoint value equals the next initial state, so the pieces are continuous; the last residual row supplies $B(y(a),y(b))=0$.

At a mesh point $t_i$, both one-sided derivatives equal $f(t_i,y(t_i))$, since each segment solves the same ODE and the joined values agree. Thus the piecewise curve is $C^1$ and solves the ODE on all of $[a,b]$; with the boundary equation it is a BVP solution.

Conversely, given a BVP solution $y$, put $s_i=y(t_i)$. On each mesh interval its restriction and the segment IVP solution have the same initial data, so uniqueness [F2] identifies them; all continuity rows vanish, and the BVP boundary condition makes the last row zero.

$$G_{h,i}(Y)=\frac{Y_{i+1}-Y_i}{h}-f\!\left(t_i+\frac h2,\frac{Y_i+Y_{i+1}}2\right)\quad(0\le i<N),\qquad G_{h,N}(Y)=B(Y_0,Y_N).$$

Fix $a<b$, an integer $d\ge1$, an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ containing $[a,b]\times$ the states under consideration, and a vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$. Let $D_B\subseteq\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $B:D_B\to\mathbb R^d$. A **square nonlinear two-point boundary-value problem (BVP)** is

$$y'(t)=f(t,y(t))\quad(a\le t\le b),\qquad B(y(a),y(b))=0,$$

where $y$ is a continuously differentiable curve whose graph lies in $\Omega$, whose endpoint pair lies in $D_B$, and where the $d$ scalar components of $B$ give exactly $d$ boundary equations. A **BVP solution** is such a curve satisfying both the differential equation and endpoint equation. No existence or uniqueness is part of this definition.

If the IVP from initial state $s\in\mathbb R^d$ has a unique solution $\phi(\cdot;s)$ on $[a,b]$, the **exact shooting residual** is $R(s):=B(s,\phi(b;s))$ whenever $(s,\phi(b;s))\in D_B$. For a mesh $a=t_0<\cdots<t_N=b$ and segment initial states $s_0,\ldots,s_N$, the **exact multiple-shooting residual** has rows $\phi_i(t_{i+1};s_i)-s_{i+1}$ for $0\le i<N$ and final row $B(s_0,s_N)$, where $\phi_i$ denotes the unique segment IVP solution when it exists. These residuals are defined only on their admissible IVP and boundary domains.

For a $d$-dimensional BVP on $[a,b]$, an integer $N\ge1$, uniform mesh width $h=(b-a)/N$, mesh nodes $t_i=a+ih$, and node vector $Y=(Y_0,\ldots,Y_N)\in(\mathbb R^d)^{N+1}$, let $D_h$ be the open set of node vectors for which every midpoint pair $(t_i+h/2,(Y_i+Y_{i+1})/2)$ lies in the vector-field domain and $(Y_0,Y_N)$ lies in the boundary-map domain. Define $G_h:D_h\to(\mathbb R^d)^{N+1}$ by

$$G_{h,i}(Y)=\frac{Y_{i+1}-Y_i}{h}-f\!\left(t_i+\frac h2,\frac{Y_i+Y_{i+1}}2\right)\quad(0\le i<N),\qquad G_{h,N}(Y)=B(Y_0,Y_N).$$

Use the maximum of the Euclidean block norms for both node and residual vectors. The interior rows are normalized by $h$; consequently an unscaled increment row has size $h$ times its normalized row.

For any $Y\in D_h$, $G_h(Y)=0$ if and only if

$$Y_{i+1}-Y_i=h f\!\left(t_i+\frac h2,\frac{Y_i+Y_{i+1}}2\right)\quad(0\le i<N),\qquad B(Y_0,Y_N)=0.$$

Equivalently, the piecewise-linear interpolant has on each segment a constant slope equal to the vector field at the segment midpoint state and satisfies the endpoint residual.

Fix a uniform mesh and the open nodal domain $D_h$ and normalized residual $G_h$ from [[def-midpoint-collocation-residual-for-bvps]]. If $f$ and $B$ are $C^1$ on the required domains (total differentiability with continuous derivative entries), then $G_h$ is a $C^1$ square map from the open subset $D_h\subseteq\mathbb R^{d(N+1)}$ into $\mathbb R^{d(N+1)}$. Given an initial node vector $Y_0\in D_h$, tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and correction budget $M\in\mathbb N_0$, apply [[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] to $G_h$ using its exact Jacobian. Return the last node vector and its root, singular-jacobian, invalid-trial, or iteration-budget-exhausted status as defined by that procedure. A root status means only that $\|G_h(Y)\|\le\tau$; it is not a branch, convergence, or error certificate.

derivations.claim: Since $y'=0$, every BVP solution is constant; the boundary equation is $y(0)^2-1=0$, whose real roots are $1$ and $-1$. Both constant curves satisfy the equation and endpoint condition.

At a residual zero, the interior rows from [F2] force $Y_{i+1}=Y_i$ for every $i$, so all nodes equal some $c$; the endpoint row then gives $c^2-1=0$. Thus the only residual zeros are the two constant node vectors $Y_i=1$ and $Y_i=-1$, in accord with [F3].

At either root, a vector $z=(z_0,\ldots,z_N)$ in the kernel of the residual Jacobian satisfies $z_{i+1}-z_i=0$ in every interior row, hence all $z_i=c$. The boundary row is $2Y_0z_0=0$; since $Y_0=\pm1$, this forces $c=0$. The square Jacobian has trivial kernel, so it is invertible and each root is simple.

Fact [F4] defines a finite Newton procedure but makes no branch-selection or global-convergence claim. The existence of both roots shows directly that the BVP and its collocation residual have no unique global solution branch.

derivations.claim: The substitution $w=u+1$ gives $w''=\lambda^2w$ with $w(0)=0$ and $w(1)=1$. Solving this constant-coefficient equation gives $w(t)=\sinh(\lambda t)/\sinh\lambda$, so $u(t)=w(t)-1\in[-1,0]$ because $\sinh(\lambda t)$ increases from $0$ to $\sinh\lambda$. Its initial slope is $s^*=w'(0)=\lambda/\sinh\lambda$.

If the initial slope is $s^*+\delta$ while $u(0)=-1$ remains fixed, linearity of the equation for $w$ gives $w_\delta(t)=(s^*+\delta)\sinh(\lambda t)/\lambda$. Subtracting the exact shot yields $w_\delta(1)-w(1)=\delta\sinh\lambda/\lambda$.

Since $\sinh\lambda-\lambda$ has value zero at $0$ and derivative $\cosh\lambda-1>0$ for $\lambda>0$, we have $\sinh\lambda/\lambda>1$. Also the derivative of $q(\lambda)=\sinh\lambda/\lambda$ has numerator $g(\lambda)=\lambda\cosh\lambda-\sinh\lambda$, where $g(0)=0$ and $g\prime(\lambda)=\lambda\sinh\lambda>0$; hence $q$ is increasing. For $\lambda\ge2$, $\sinh\lambda\ge e^{\lambda-1}/2$, so $q(\lambda)\ge e^{\lambda-1}/(2\lambda)\to\infty$. The perturbed terminal boundary residual vector changes by $(0,\delta\sinh\lambda/\lambda)$, while [F2]–[F3] identify this as the endpoint residual evaluated by exact single shooting.
